title: Patterns, Sleep, Drugs and Activation
subtitle: Domain II quick review: polarity and measurement, benign variants, sleep, neonatal EEG, medication effects and activation procedures

tabs.title: Polarity and Measurement
tabs.intro: Every differential amplifier compares input 1 with input 2, and the pen direction tells you which input was more negative. Most Domain II reading errors come from forgetting that rule, from misreading sensitivity, or from mixing up period and frequency. Work the numbers until they are automatic.

sections.title: The negative-up convention
head: Situation
Pen direction
Why
rows: The EEG convention: relative negativity at input 1 deflects upward
A negative event that lands in input 2 looks like a positive one in that channel
Positivity at input 2 is read as relative negativity at input 1
A differential amplifier only shows the difference; an event equally present at both inputs disappears
sections.note: So a surface-negative wave is not always an upward deflection. Its direction depends on which input it reaches more strongly in that derivation.

sections.title: Polarity of common waveforms (at the scalp)
head: Waveform
Usual surface polarity
Memory hook
rows: Large vertex negativity in N1 to N2
BETS / small sharp spikes, wicket spikes
The word positive is in the name
Small negative, then the largest positive phase, then a slower negative
The dominant middle phase is positive

QRS-locked sharp transients, usually largest on the left (left ear A1 and left temporal and posterior leads); ABRET describes the R wave as positive over the left posterior quadrant, but the displayed polarity depends on the montage
The heart's axis points down and left, so left-sided electrodes (especially the left ear) see it most
The cornea is positive and rolls up toward Fp electrodes (Bell phenomenon)

cards.title: Bipolar montage: phase reversal
cards.body: Find the electrode shared by two adjacent channels where the deflections flip direction. That shared electrode is the maximum.
points: Negative event: the two pens point toward each other
Positive event: the two pens point away from each other
End-of-chain problem: if the maximum is at the first or last electrode of a chain there is no reversal; check with a referential montage

cards.title: Referential montage: amplitude
cards.body: Every channel shares one reference, so the channel with the largest deflection marks the maximum. No phase reversal is expected unless the reference itself is active.
points: An active reference puts the same wave in every channel, sometimes in the opposite direction
A quiet channel can mean the electrode and reference carry equal potential

cards.title: Choosing a reference
cards.body: Pick a reference far from the activity of interest. For temporal discharges, Cz is a good choice because ear electrodes pick up temporal activity themselves.
points: Cz is a poor reference for vertex waves, spindles and central activity
Ear references are contaminated by mid and anterior temporal discharges and by ECG

sections.title: Measuring voltage: deflection (mm) x sensitivity (uV/mm)
head: Measured peak-to-peak
Sensitivity
Voltage
rows: Deflection shrinks from 10 mm to 5 mm; the voltage is unchanged
sections.note: Measure from the trough to the peak of the wave you are asked about, in the channel shown. The smaller the uV/mm number, the more sensitive the setting: 2 uV/mm draws a wave 2.5 times taller than 5 uV/mm.

sections.title: Frequency and duration
items: Frequency (Hz) = number of complete waves in 1 second; period = 1 / frequency.
At 30 mm/s paper speed, 1 s = 30 mm, so a wave 6 mm wide lasts 200 ms and repeats at 5 Hz.
Duration bands: spike 20 to under 70 ms; sharp wave 70 to 200 ms.
Bands: delta under 4 Hz, theta 4 to under 8 Hz, alpha 8 to 13 Hz, beta over 13 Hz.
Count waves over a full second, not one cycle, when the rhythm is irregular.
On digital review, check the displayed time base (seconds per page) before you count.

cards.title: 60 Hz notch
cards.body: One cycle of 60 Hz lasts 1/60 s = about 16.7 ms. A notch filter strips energy near 60 Hz, so a waveform about 16 to 17 ms wide is attenuated most; a 50 ms wave is barely touched.
points: Spikes are fast, so a notch can blunt their peaks
Fix the 60 Hz source (impedance, grounds, cords) before reaching for the notch
Where mains is 50 Hz, the matching period is 20 ms

cards.title: High-frequency filter (low-pass)
cards.body: Lowering it (for example 70 to 15 Hz) shrinks fast activity and can make muscle look like beta or round off spikes.

cards.title: Low-frequency filter (high-pass)
cards.body: Raising it (for example 1 to 5 Hz) shrinks slow waves and can hide focal delta.

pearls: A negative event at input 2 deflects down: never call a wave positive from its direction alone.
Negative phase reversal: pens point toward each other at the shared electrode.
2 uV/mm is more sensitive than 5 uV/mm; the smaller number gives the bigger trace.
Voltage = mm x uV/mm. Changing sensitivity changes the drawing, never the voltage.
60 Hz notch: 1/60 s = 16.7 ms, so the shortest (about 16 ms) waveform is affected most.
ECG artifact is time-locked to the QRS, usually largest over the left ear and left temporal and posterior leads, and can look like spikes; add an ECG channel to prove it.
Lennox-Gastaut slow spike-and-wave runs at about 1.5 to 2.5 Hz; classic absence spike-wave is about 3 Hz.
Use Cz, not the ears, as the reference when the question is temporal spikes.
tabs.eegLink: Before marking any spike, confirm its polarity and field across two montages and note the sensitivity and filters in use.

tabs.title: Benign Variants
tabs.intro: Benign variants look sharp or rhythmic but carry no link to epilepsy. Each has a typical age, state and location; matching those three details is how you tell them from true epileptiform discharges. A second group of rhythmic or periodic patterns looks similar but is not benign.

sections.title: Benign variants at a glance
head: Variant
Age
State
Location
Polarity
How to tell from epileptiform
rows: BETS (benign epileptiform transients of sleep) = small sharp spikes
Drowsiness and light sleep; gone in deep sleep
Temporal, wide field, often bilateral independent
Low amplitude (under about 50 uV), very brief, little or no after-going slow wave, no background disruption; often opposite polarity over the other hemisphere
Arch-shaped 6 to 11 Hz runs; a single wicket matches the shape of the waves in the run, has no slow wave and does not disturb the background
Comb-like bursts under 1 s at 14 and/or 6 Hz; best seen in a referential montage with wide spacing (for example contralateral ear)
Awake and drowsy; fades in deeper sleep
Brief 1 to 2 s bursts at 5 to 7 Hz with a very small spike; WHAM features raise concern, FOLD features favor benign
Rhythmic midtemporal theta of drowsiness (psychomotor variant)
Notched or flat-topped 5 to 7 Hz trains that stay monomorphic and do not evolve in frequency or field
SREDA (subclinical rhythmic EEG discharge of adults)
Abrupt onset, lasts tens of seconds to minutes, no clinical change, no postictal slowing; patient can talk normally during it
Awake, eyes open, scanning a picture or text
Vanish with eyes closed or a blank card; triangular, time-locked to saccades
Checkmark shape, often in 4 to 5 Hz runs, only in sleep
Any age; common in young people
7 to 11 Hz comb; blocked by moving or planning to move the opposite limb, not by eye opening
Infants and children (about 3 months to early teens)
High-amplitude 3 to 5 Hz runs that may have sharp notches but no true spikes, appearing only at state change
Block with eye opening along with the alpha and disappear in sleep
Slow variant is a notched half-frequency of alpha; fast variant is double; both block with eye opening like alpha
Any age after craniotomy or skull defect
Higher amplitude and faster than the other side; check the history. Focal slowing under it still counts

sections.title: Look-alikes that are NOT benign
head: Pattern
Typical patient
What it looks like
What it suggests
Technologist action
rows: Runs of about 3 Hz rhythmic delta over both occipital areas, blocked by eye opening, often increased by HV
Associated with childhood absence epilepsy; not a benign variant
Run full HV and watch for generalized 3 Hz spike-wave; test responsiveness
Bursts of 1.5 to 3 Hz rhythmic frontal delta, often in drowsiness, attenuated by alerting
Nonspecific encephalopathy: toxic-metabolic, raised intracranial pressure, deep midline lesions
Document mental status, medications and alerting tests
Runs of rhythmic delta over one temporal region
Strongly linked to temporal lobe epilepsy; treated like an interictal epileptiform finding
Add sleep and anterior temporal electrodes per protocol
Sharp or spike complexes repeating at roughly regular intervals (often about 1 per second) over one hemisphere
Acute structural injury (stroke, HSV encephalitis, tumor) and high seizure risk
Notify per critical-value protocol; watch for evolution to seizure

sections.title: Telling benign from epileptiform: checklist
items: Note age and state: most sharp variants live in drowsiness and light sleep.
Look for an after-going slow wave and background disruption; true discharges usually have both.
Check the field: true spikes have a physiologic field over several electrodes; very narrow or shifting fields suggest a variant or artifact.
Check morphology across the run: a variant repeats one stable shape; a seizure evolves in frequency, amplitude and field.
Confirm polarity in two montages; positive sharp transients in an adult are usually variants (POSTS, lambda, 14 and 6).
Mark and describe; leave interpretation to the reader.

pearls: BETS and small sharp spikes are the same pattern: adult, light sleep, low and brief, no slow wave.
Lambda is awake and visual; POSTS is the sleeping cousin. Both are occipital and positive.
Mu is blocked by contralateral movement, alpha by eye opening.
6 Hz phantom spike-wave: WHAM is worrisome, FOLD is benign.
OIRDA is not benign: in a child it points toward absence epilepsy. Posterior slow waves of youth are the benign occipital pattern.
SREDA is rhythmic and long but the patient stays normal and there is no postictal slowing.
Hypnagogic hypersynchrony in a 4-year-old at sleep onset is normal; the same burst while fully awake is not.
tabs.eegLink: Mislabeling a benign variant as epileptiform can lead to wrong diagnoses, so write the age, state and location next to any sharp transient you mark.

tabs.title: Sleep
tabs.intro: Sleep raises the yield of epileptiform discharges, and its normal transients mature on a timetable. Know the adult stages, when each sleep feature appears in infancy, and which extra channels to add when the patient's sleep looks disordered.

sections.title: Adult sleep staging features
head: Stage
EEG
Eyes and EMG
rows: Alpha drops out; low-voltage mixed theta; vertex waves; POSTS may begin
Slow rolling eye movements; tone slightly lower
Sleep spindles (about 11 to 14 Hz, 0.5 to 2 s, maximal central) and K-complexes on a theta background
Usually no eye movements (slow rolling movements may persist early in N2)
High-amplitude delta (about 0.5 to 2 Hz, over 75 uV peak-to-peak) in at least 20% of the epoch, frontal maximum
Low-voltage mixed frequency like N1; sawtooth waves at the vertex; alpha may appear 1 to 2 Hz slower than waking alpha
Rapid eye movements; chin EMG at its lowest (atonia); brief twitches; irregular breathing

sections.title: Development of sleep features
head: Feature
First appears
Notes
rows: Long trains in infancy; asynchronous between hemispheres in the first year is normal
Should be synchronous by about 2 years
Persistent asynchrony after about 2 years is abnormal; a consistently absent spindle on one side is abnormal at any age after they develop
Become sharper and taller through childhood
From a few months of age
Newborns enter sleep through active (REM-like) sleep
By about 3 months, sleep onset is through NREM; REM at onset in an adult is abnormal

sections.title: Sleep disorders and what to add

cards.title: Obstructive sleep apnea
cards.body: Repeated arousals with snoring, pauses in breathing and desaturation. Add respiratory monitoring: airflow, chest/abdominal effort and pulse oximetry per protocol.
points: Chin EMG alone does not show apnea
Document each arousal and what preceded it

cards.title: Narcolepsy
cards.body: Sleep-onset REM: REM appearing within about 15 minutes of falling asleep. Eye leads and chin EMG let you prove REM.
points: Formal testing is the MSLT, which looks for short sleep latency and two or more sleep-onset REM periods

cards.title: NREM parasomnias
cards.body: Sleepwalking, sleep terrors and confusional arousals come out of N3, usually in the first third of the night.
points: Video plus EEG separates them from nocturnal frontal lobe seizures

cards.title: REM sleep behavior disorder
cards.body: Dream-enactment because REM atonia is lost. Chin and limb EMG show tone during REM.
points: Video is essential
May precede Parkinson disease and related disorders

cards.title: Periodic limb movements
cards.body: Repetitive leg jerks during sleep, often with arousals. Add anterior tibialis surface EMG on both legs.
points: Movements recur at fairly regular intervals of seconds

pearls: Spindles: 11 to 16 Hz (most 12 to 14 Hz) bursts lasting 0.5 s or more, maximal centrally, in N2.
Spindle asynchrony is normal in infancy and abnormal after about 2 years.
An adult who keeps waking with snoring needs respiration and oximetry, not just muscle tone.
REM within about 15 minutes of sleep onset in an adult suggests narcolepsy: document it with eye and chin channels.
Sawtooth waves belong to REM; POSTS and vertex waves to N1 and N2.
N3 needs high-amplitude delta in at least a fifth of the epoch.
tabs.eegLink: When sleep looks abnormal, add the right polygraphic channel early and annotate the event; the reader cannot reconstruct what was not recorded.

tabs.title: Neonatal EEG
tabs.intro: Neonatal EEG is read against conceptional age and state. Polygraphy (eyes, chin EMG, respiration, ECG) is needed to identify state, and many patterns that are normal at one age are abnormal at another.

cards.title: Tracé discontinu (preterm)
cards.body: Bursts of activity separated by very low-amplitude interburst periods. The gaps shorten as the baby matures.
points: Normal in preterm infants
In a term baby a similar pattern is abnormal

cards.title: Tracé alternant (term quiet sleep)
cards.body: High-voltage bursts alternate with lower but still clearly active periods lasting a few seconds.
points: Emerges in the mid-30s weeks
Replaced by continuous slow-wave sleep by about 44 to 46 weeks

cards.title: Continuous
cards.body: Activity without gaps. At term, active sleep and wakefulness are continuous.
points: Burst suppression (invariant, unreactive) is abnormal at any age

sections.title: Delta brushes by conceptional age
head: Conceptional age
Delta brushes
rows: Peak abundance; spread to temporal and occipital areas
Rare; should be gone by about 44 weeks
sections.note: A delta brush is a delta wave with fast (beta-range) activity riding on it. Many brushes in a term or post-term infant suggest immaturity or dysfunction.

sections.title: Sharp transients: normal vs abnormal
head: Transient
Normal
Abnormal
rows: Diphasic, often bilateral and synchronous, in transitional/light sleep from about 34 to 35 weeks to a few weeks after term
Very frequent, consistently one-sided or persisting well past term
Occasional, random, bilateral independent, in sleep
Persistent, repetitive, consistently lateralized, in runs, or present in wakefulness near term; a nonspecific sign of dysfunction on that side
Associated with white matter injury in preterm infants

sections.title: Conceptional age arithmetic
items: Conceptional age (CA) = gestational age at birth + time since birth (legal age).
Born at 30 weeks, now 6 weeks old: CA = 36 weeks.
Born at 34 weeks, now 4 weeks old: CA = 38 weeks; compare with term norms, not with a 4-week-old term baby.
Born at term (40 weeks), now 8 weeks old: CA = 48 weeks; spindles should be emerging.

Write gestational age, legal age and the sum on the requisition. ACNS now uses postmenstrual age (PMA = gestational age + chronological age) for this sum; older EEG texts called the same number conceptional age.

pearls: Active sleep: eye movements, twitches, absent chin EMG, irregular breathing.
Quiet sleep at term shows tracé alternant; preterm quiet sleep shows tracé discontinu.
Right temporal sharp transients during wakefulness at 38 weeks CA are a nonspecific sign of right temporal dysfunction: not normal, not proof of epilepsy.
Encoches frontales are normal frontal sharp transients near term.
Delta brushes are the hallmark of prematurity and should fade by term.
Without eye, chin, respiration and ECG channels, neonatal state cannot be scored.
tabs.eegLink: Record long enough to capture a full sleep cycle (usually about an hour) and annotate state changes, because the reader judges each pattern against state and CA.

tabs.title: Medications
tabs.intro: Drugs change the background, the fast activity and sometimes the epileptiform findings. Expect a question to give a drug history and a pattern and ask what explains it or what to document.

sections.title: Drug effects on the EEG
head: Drug or class
Usual EEG effect
Toxicity or withdrawal
rows: Increased beta, often frontal; drowsiness; may suppress epileptiform discharges
Abrupt withdrawal: seizures and photoparoxysmal responses
Increased beta; high doses give slowing, burst suppression and even electrocerebral silence
Withdrawal is classically linked to photoparoxysmal responses and seizures; intoxication must be excluded before ECI testing
Toxicity: diffuse slowing; clinically nystagmus first, then ataxia and slurred speech as levels rise
Toxicity slows the background; can aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures
Reduces generalized spike-wave and photoparoxysmal responses
High ammonia can cause encephalopathy with slowing and triphasic waves
Mild slowing even at therapeutic levels
Toxicity: diffuse slowing, triphasic waves, sharp or periodic discharges
Lower the seizure threshold; overdose causes slowing and epileptiform activity
Slowing; clozapine can produce epileptiform discharges
Overdose: marked slowing; meperidine metabolite can cause seizures
Beta at light sedation, then slowing and burst suppression with deeper doses
Used to treat refractory status epilepticus
Increased fast activity and theta rather than typical sedative slowing
Can make the record look less sedated than the patient is
Acute: mild slowing; chronic: lower voltage
Withdrawal: seizures and enhanced photic (photomyogenic or photoparoxysmal) responses
Remove muscle artifact; also hide clinical seizure signs, so EEG is the only seizure monitor
Can reduce drowsiness and increase fast activity
Can make sleep hard to obtain; high doses lower seizure threshold

sections.title: What to document
items: Every current medication with dose and time of last dose, especially anti-seizure drugs and sedatives.
Sedation given for the test: drug, dose, route, time and who gave it, per facility policy.
Recent stopping or tapering of benzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol or anti-seizure drugs.
Paralytics: note that muscle artifact is gone because of the drug, not because the patient is calm.
Changes in the record that follow a dose (for example new beta 10 minutes after lorazepam).

cards.title: Diffuse excess beta
cards.body: Think sedative or hypnotic drug first: benzodiazepine or barbiturate.
points: A focal lack of beta can point to cortical dysfunction or fluid over the cortex on that side

cards.title: Triphasic waves
cards.body: Metabolic: hepatic, renal, lithium toxicity, hyperammonemia from valproate.

cards.title: New photoparoxysmal response
cards.body: Ask about recent sedative or alcohol withdrawal.

cards.title: Clean record in an intubated ICU patient
cards.body: Check whether a neuromuscular blocker is running; record its name and time.

pearls: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates are the classic causes of excess beta.
Barbiturate withdrawal is the drug state most associated with photic-induced epileptiform discharges.
Nystagmus is the earliest and ataxia the most disabling clinical sign of phenytoin toxicity.
Lithium toxicity can produce triphasic waves even when the serum level looks acceptable.
Rocuronium has no cerebral effect; it only removes muscle artifact.
Exclude sedative intoxication and hypothermia before an ECI study.
tabs.eegLink: A drug and timing note on the record lets the reader separate medication effect from new pathology.

tabs.title: Activation
tabs.intro: Photic stimulation, hyperventilation and sleep deprivation are the standard activations. Know the normal responses, the atypical ones you must note, when to stop, and when not to start.

sections.title: Photic stimulation: set-up
items: Place the lamp about 30 cm (12 inches) from the nasion, in a dimmed room.
Step through flash rates from low to high (for example 1 to about 30 Hz) in short trains per lab protocol.
Record with eyes open and eyes closed during trains; eye closure itself can trigger responses in some patients.
Mark each flash rate on the record; event markers show time-locking.
Keep photic separate from the hyperventilation recovery period.

sections.title: Photic responses
head: Response
What you see
Meaning
rows: Occipital waves at the flash rate, time-locked, usually best near alpha frequencies
Normal; its absence is also normal
Occipital response at a multiple of the flash rate
Response at a fraction (for example half) of the flash rate
Clear driving on one side, little on the other
Atypical: the side with less response may be dysfunctional; note it
High-amplitude occipital responses to 1 to 3 Hz flashes
Atypical beyond early childhood; note it, especially if large or spiky (for example in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis)
Frontal muscle spikes time-locked to each flash, about 50 ms later; stop when flashes stop; reduced by opening the eyes
Muscle, not brain; seen with anxiety and in drug or alcohol withdrawal
Generalized spikes or spike-wave, not strictly time-locked
Stops with the flash vs continues after it
Self-sustained (outlasting) responses are more strongly linked to epilepsy

sections.title: When to stop photic
items: Stop the flashes as soon as a generalized photoparoxysmal response appears; do not run the full train.
Stop for any clinical seizure, and follow seizure first aid and notification per protocol.
Note the flash rate and eye state at which the response began.

cards.title: Normal response
cards.body: Deep breathing for about 3 to 5 minutes lowers CO2 and constricts cerebral vessels. Diffuse slowing builds up, most in children and young adults and with low blood sugar.
points: Slowing should settle within about a minute after HV stops
Record at least a minute of recovery

cards.title: Abnormal response
cards.body: Focal or asymmetric slowing, epileptiform discharges, or slowing that persists or returns after HV stops.
points: Moyamoya: slowing that reappears after HV (re-build-up) is typical
3 Hz spike-wave with staring: test responsiveness (give a word to recall)

cards.title: Contraindications
cards.body: Decided by the ordering physician and lab policy.
points: Recent stroke, TIA, or intracranial hemorrhage
Moyamoya and sickle cell disease
Significant heart or lung disease, uncontrolled hypertension
Raised intracranial pressure; a patient who cannot cooperate

sections.title: Sleep deprivation and reflex activations
items: Sleep deprivation raises the yield of interictal discharges, especially generalized (for example juvenile myoclonic epilepsy) and temporal ones; the patient should not drive afterward.
Reflex triggers tested only when the history suggests them: reading, music, startle, striped patterns, video games, eating, hot water, mental arithmetic, eye closure.
Record the exact stimulus and the patient's behavior with the EEG change.

sections.title: Related tests in one line
head: Test
What it does
rows: Briefly anesthetizes one hemisphere to show which side holds language and memory before surgery; EEG confirms the drug effect
A blood-flow tracer; injected during a seizure (ictal SPECT) it shows increased flow at the focus
Shows glucose metabolism; the focus is usually hypometabolic between seizures
Maps language and motor areas through blood-oxygen changes without radiation
Records the brain's magnetic fields to localize spike sources
Averaged responses to repeated stimuli test conduction in visual, auditory and sensory pathways

pearls: Driving at the flash rate is normal; beyond early childhood, large driving at delta flash rates or marked asymmetry is atypical.
Photomyogenic responses are frontal, flash-locked muscle and stop with the flashes; photoparoxysmal responses are cerebral spike-wave.
Stop flashing at the first generalized photoparoxysmal response.
Slowing that lingers or returns after HV suggests cerebrovascular disease such as moyamoya.
Sickle cell disease and recent stroke are HV contraindications.
Wada = intracarotid amobarbital to lateralize language and memory.
tabs.eegLink: Annotate every activation step (flash rate, eye state, HV start and stop, patient effort) so the reader can tie each change to its trigger.

mistakes: A surface-negative wave always deflects up.
It deflects up only at input 1; at input 2 it deflects down.
5 uV/mm is more sensitive than 2 uV/mm.
The smaller number is more sensitive; 2 uV/mm draws a taller wave.
Voltage is the millimeters measured.
Voltage = mm x uV/mm; 8 mm at 7 uV/mm is 56 uV.
A 60 Hz notch affects a 50 ms wave most.
It affects waves near 1/60 s (about 16.7 ms) most.
Spindle asynchrony is never abnormal.
It is normal in infancy but abnormal after about 2 years.
A patient with repeated arousals needs chin EMG.
Suspected sleep apnea needs respiration and oximetry monitoring.
Photomyogenic is the atypical photic response.
Photomyogenic is muscle artifact; beyond early childhood, large driving at delta flash rates or marked asymmetry is atypical.
Temporal sharp transients are always normal in neonates.
Persistent, lateralized ones or ones in wakefulness at term suggest dysfunction on that side.
OIRDA is a benign variant.
OIRDA in children is linked to absence epilepsy; posterior slow waves of youth are the benign pattern.
Triphasic waves are mainly surface-negative.
The largest phase of a triphasic wave is positive.
Cz is a poor reference for temporal spikes.
Cz is far from the temporal lobes; ear references pick up temporal activity.
Rocuronium slows the EEG.
Neuromuscular blockers have no cerebral effect; they only remove muscle artifact.
Photic-induced discharges point to phenytoin toxicity.
They are most linked to barbiturate or sedative withdrawal.
Mu rhythm blocks with eye opening.
Mu blocks with contralateral movement; alpha blocks with eye opening.
memory: Relative negativity at input 1 sends the pen up.
6 Hz phantom spike-wave: Wake, High amplitude, Anterior, Male is more concerning; Female, Occipital, Low amplitude, Drowsy is benign.
Both are occipital and positive; state tells them apart.
